summary.text: 天 means “sky” or “heaven.” Its early graph is analyzed either as a person with the head marked or as a depiction of heaven; the surviving evidence does not settle which meaning came first.

formation.text: Pictographic in the analysis that sees a standing human figure with an emphasized head: 大 depicts the person and the upper mark represents the head. Another account treats the word’s original meaning as “sky” and the human-like graph as an anthropomorphic depiction of heaven. Neither analysis identifies a sound component.

components.text: In the head-marked analysis of early 天, 大 depicts a standing person. It is a pictorial part of the graph, not a sound component.
In the same analysis, the upper mark represents the emphasized head. Paleographers describe its later reduction to a horizontal stroke.

history.text: The curated Shang-style oracle-script illustration is a modern redraw of an identified exemplar. Its person and marked head illustrate one paleographic interpretation; the image alone does not settle the character’s earliest meaning.

Paleographic accounts describe the head mark as simplified into a horizontal stroke. The Eastern Han dictionary analyzes 天 as 一 plus 大 and glosses it through 顛, “top of the head”; this is a historical interpretation, not proof of the earliest spoken meaning.

Reported Shang material includes head-related use and 天邑商 alongside 大邑商, suggesting interchange or close relation between 天 and 大 in some expressions. Later reported examples include 天命 and 天子 in bronze inscriptions, and 天命 and 天下 in Warring States texts; these contexts do not establish an unbroken path of meaning change.

A competing account takes “sky” as the original word meaning and the older human-like graph as an anthropomorphic depiction of heaven. The evidence does not resolve this disagreement or date each cited inscription precisely.

uncertainties.text: Early head-related uses, the 天/大 interchange, and the competing sky-first account do not establish a single earliest spoken sense or a complete development from head or top to sky and heaven.
The cited reconstructions use distinct systems, and early dialectal variation is reported. Neither 一 nor 大 is supported as a phonetic component of 天.

senses.text: Sky or heaven is the established meaning of 天, and one account proposes it as the word’s original meaning. Early inscription evidence and its interpretation are contested, so this records an attested sense category rather than a proven original meaning or priority over head-related use.

senses.period: Shang oracle-bone corpus; individual token dates unresolved
senses.text: A head-related use is reported in an oracle-bone context. Paleographic analyses connect it with the graph’s marked head, but its relationship to the word for sky or heaven remains unsettled.

senses.gloss: “great” or use in a name expression
senses.period: Shang-Zhou material; individual token dates unresolved
senses.text: 天邑商 is cited alongside 大邑商, and an older gloss reads 天 as “great” in one phrase. This supports early interchange or close relation in usage, not an original meaning of “great.”

senses.gloss: divine or sovereign uses, including “Heaven” in compounds
senses.period: Bronze inscriptions and later Warring States texts; individual token dates unresolved
senses.text: Reported examples include 天帝, 天命, 天子, and 天下. Their contexts attest divine, sovereign, or “under heaven” uses, but compound meanings alone do not establish separate single-character senses or a dated sequence of change.

developments.text: One paleographic analysis proposes extension from the head or head-top association to the sky above. A competing account treats “sky” as original; the chronology remains unresolved.

limitations.text: The cited inscriptions lack verified absolute dates for each token. The evidence does not establish one certain earliest spoken sense or a complete semantic sequence; earliest graph attestation and earliest spoken meaning are separate questions.

overview.text: 天 means “sky” or “heaven.” One analysis sees a standing person with the head marked; another takes “sky” as the original meaning. The early evidence does not settle which came first.

components.text: The lower shape depicts a standing person in one analysis of the old graph.
The upper mark is interpreted as the emphasized head and is described as later simplified into a horizontal stroke.

relationships.text: In the head-marked analysis, 大 depicts the standing person in the early graph.
Paleographic analyses interpret the upper mark as the person’s emphasized head and describe its later reduction to a horizontal stroke.
